newsitem.title: UK: Catholic leaders urge IRA to call new truce.
newsitem.headline: Catholic leaders urge IRA to call new truce.

text.p: Roman Catholic leaders piled pressure on IRA guerrillas on Tuesday to call a truce and salvage Northern Ireland's faltering peace process.

Cardinal Cahal Daly, retiring as spiritual head of the island's five million Catholics, said violence by the Irish Republican Army was the chief obstacle to its Sinn Fein political arm getting a place at peace talks.
"No single thing would do more at this time to restore hope and lessen division in our society than a reinstatement of the IRA ceasefire," Daly told reporters in Armagh, west of Belfast.

Daly described a decision by convicted pro-British Loyalist guerrillas to end their support for the two-year peace efforts as disturbing but said it should not signal a breakdown of a Loyalist two-year truce and a return to sectarian violence.
"I am still confident that nobody will be so reckless, so irresponsible as to plunge this country again into the madness and the agony of violence from which we have so recently escaped."

The Loyalist prisoners' decision, following a string of IRA bomb attacks in mainland Britain and a foiled bomb attack by republican dissidents in Belfast, has heightened fears that pro-British Protestant gunmen might resume hostilities against Catholics who want a United Ireland.

Also appealing for an IRA ceasefire, leading Catholic politician Seamus Mallon, deputy leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP), said the Loyalists' statement that they had lost confidence in peace moves had created a "serious situation, a potential threat to the peace process."

Protestant extremists answered an Irish Republican Army (IRA) truce in September 1994 with their own ceasefire in October. The IRA ended their truce with bombs in London in February but the Protestant guerrilla ceasefire still holds.
"I believe they (the IRA) have it in their power to ensure that the apprehension in the community recedes and that the peace process can be built on," Mallon told reporters in Belfast.
A politician linked to the pro-British Loyalist guerrillas warned earlier that sectarian bloodshed could return to Northern Ireland if IRA guerrillas launched more attacks.

"If there is any reaction from Sinn Fein/IRA, then it makes it much more difficult and there is every likelihood that there could be a return to full-scale conflict," said John White, leader of the Ulster Democratic Party.
Around 1,000 Loyalist and IRA prisoners in Belfast are frustrated that Britain did not respond to the 1994 ceasefires by announcing an amnesty.
Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring said he could understand the frustration felt by prisoners but violence was not the answer.
"I certainly would hope that it is not a return to violence because once violence resumes on their side then I think the scenario becomes very bleak on all sides," he told Irish radio.

IRA bombs in Britain, and discoveries such as last week's haul of 10 tonnes of explosives in London, have fed fears that despite talk of peace the IRA remains as determined as ever to use force to end British rule.
The IRA's political wing Sinn Fein have been excluded from multi-party talks on the political future of the province -- still bogged down in procedural matters -- until the IRA renews its ceasefire.
